excerpt: Energy projects are often framed as technical problems of supply, infrastructure, cost, and risk. That framing is necessary but incomplete because energy systems also organize relationships among institutions, communities, land, water, livelihoods, and future generations.
body:
In ENVS 839, I have been reflecting on Two-Eyed Seeing, Ethical Space, relational systems thinking, the Four Rs, and research on Indigenous involvement and control in renewable energy. A central lesson for me is that good engineering and ethical engagement are not competing priorities. The deeper challenge is deciding who defines the problem, what knowledge is recognized, how authority is shared, and what success means.

This has changed how I revisit an electrification proposal discussed in my Assignment 2 for a swamp community near oil & gas operations in Nigeria. The proposal involved moving from diesel generation toward gas, with two 1 MW gas generators procured. Reliability, reduced diesel reliance, safe gas use, and future renewable integration were intended goals and questions. No project outcomes or community responses were established, so I cannot present the technology choice as proof of sustainability.



## Key takeaways

> Stakeholderengagement should not begin after the problem and preferred solution arealready fixed. Community knowledge and locally legitimate authority should helpshape project purpose, options, governance, risk analysis, knowledge and datarules, and measures of success.
>
>

*As I continue developing in energy security and project leadership, I am asking: How can project teams protect schedule and technical rigour while remaining genuinely open to co-learning that may change the project itself?*

Thank you, Dr Elaina Guilmette, for guiding this learning.

title: Two-Eyed Seeing (Etuaptmumk): Technical certainty can arrive too early in an energy project.
